profiles.title: Blanco tequila, Tequila Valley style
profiles.context: Blanco tequila born in the town of Tequila and the valley that carries its name, from 100% blue agave grown in this same ground. Valley conditions — lower elevation, warmer nights — tend to grow smaller, more herbaceous agave than Los Altos, so valley blancos often read savory and vegetal rather than sweet: the taste of this soil, a distinction the valley is proud of.
profiles.description: A blanco (also called silver or plata) is tequila bottled without oak aging, so what reaches the glass is the distilled character of the cooked agave itself: roasted piña, citrus, pepper and fresh vegetal notes.
profiles.finish: Clean and peppery, with citrus and a gentle vegetal warmth that fades steadily.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked (oven/autoclave), tahona or roller-mill extraction, fermented in open tanks, double distilled; typically unaged, though blanco rules permit brief oak contact below the two-month reposado minimum
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; blanco is a legal class of tequila typically sold unaged, though the rules permit brief oak maturation below the reposado minimum
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tequila? Start here: no barrel stands between you and the cooked agave, so a blanco is the clearest introduction to how each producer's land reads in the glass.

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass or with a lime wheel; also the classic Margarita and Paloma base. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.

profiles.whyItTastes: The savory, earthy edge is place plus method working together: valley agave tends to grow smaller and more herbaceous than highland agave (a tendency, not a rule), and traditional valley producers crush the cooked piña with a tahona stone wheel and ferment in open tanks. Age and price explain none of it; method and place together shape the glass, neither alone decides it.

profiles.title: Espadín mezcal, Valles Centrales style
profiles.context: Artisanal joven mezcal made from espadín agave (Agave angustifolia) in the Valles Centrales around Oaxaca. Here mezcal is family work: agave hearts roasted in earthen pit ovens, small batches, each palenque passing its craft to the next generation. The pit roast gives the spirit its signature smoke — in the Valles Centrales that smoke is part of home, the taste of the land itself, and locals embrace it as such. Espadín is the most widely planted mezcal agave — the one a Oaxacan family pours first for a curious visitor, because it is the friendliest way into the tradition.
profiles.description: Mezcal is a distilled spirit made from the cooked hearts of many agave species, not just blue agave. This profile describes an artisanal pit-roasted style: roasting the piñas underground gives this style its smoke, though not all mezcal is pit-roasted or smoky, layered over fruit, herb and mineral notes that vary with the agave variety, the village and the maestro mezcalero. This profile describes the style of a typical Valles Centrales espadín joven; individual bottles vary widely.
profiles.smoke: Gentle to moderate smoke from the pit-roast, woven through the fruit and herb notes rather than dominating them.
profiles.finish: Long and dry, with smoke that lingers softly and fades into earthy herbs.
profiles.process: Earthen-pit roast, tahona or horse-drawn mill, wild-yeast fermentation, double distilled, joven (unaged)
profiles.category: Mezcal — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; joven/abocado is an unaged legal class
profiles.beginnerNote: New to mezcal? The smoke comes from roasting the agave underground — it is a character of the process, not an added flavor. Oaxacans will happily tell you it is the taste of their earth.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat at room temperature; smoke opens up in a wide glass. Editor's suggestion only.

profiles.whyItTastes: The earthen-pit roast cooks espadín slowly over wood — that is where the roast character comes from (how much smoke varies with wood, time and pit). Wild-yeast fermentation and tahona milling add texture; joven means no oak stands between you and the cook.

profiles.title: Bacanora, Agave Pacifica style (Sierra de Sonora)
profiles.context: Bacanora is Sonora's own wild agave spirit: distilled from Agave angustifolia pacifica (locally called Pacifica, or Yaquiana) in the Sierra Madre de Sonora, under a denomination of origin that covers 35 Sonoran municipalities. For most of the 20th century (1915–1992, per Sonoran official history) making it was prohibited, and distilling continued quietly in the sierra; production was legalized again in 1992 and the denomination of origin arrived in 2000 — two separate milestones. That continuity is the heart of the tradition: bacanora survived because families kept distilling it, in vinatas passed from one generation of vinateros to the next.
profiles.description: Traditional bacanora roasts the agave hearts in earthen pit ovens, often with mesquite wood, ferments with wild yeasts and distills twice, giving a spirit that sits stylistically between tequila and Oaxacan mezcal: roasted agave at the center with smoke that is usually gentler than mezcal's, plus desert herbs and a mineral edge from the Sierra.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia pacifica (wild-harvested; locally Pacifica or Yaquiana)
profiles.process: Pit-roasted (often mesquite-fueled), wild-yeast fermentation, double distillation
profiles.category: Bacanora — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Sonora, since 2000)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to bacanora? Think of it as mezcal's Sonoran cousin — same roasted-agave heart, usually a touch less smoky, often leaner and more herbal.
profiles.smoke: Present but usually gentler than Oaxacan mezcal: the pit roast gives a lean, savory smoke rather than a dominant one.
profiles.finish: Dry and herbal, with a soft smoky thread and a mineral, peppery fade.

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass; a short rest opens the roast aromas. A little water or one ice cube works too if you prefer it softer. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.

profiles.whyItTastes: Wild Pacifica/Yaquiana agave from the Sonoran sierra, pit-roasted (often over mesquite) and wild-fermented: reviewers and producers describe an herbal, gently smoky character that the guide attributes to the plant and the pit roast together — a documented tendency of this style, not a guaranteed outcome of wild harvest. Double distillation is the standard method here; it does not by itself ensure cleanliness.

profiles.title: Sierra raicilla, Maximiliana style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Raicilla is the mountain spirit of Jalisco (the DO also reaches one Nayarit municipality, awarded in 2019), and jaliscienses wear it as proof their state makes more than tequila. It splits into two editorial traditions: Sierra (mountain) raicilla, made mainly from Agave maximiliana and inaequidens cooked in above-ground ovens, and Costa (coastal) raicilla from angustifolia and rhodacantha cooked in underground pits. For decades raicilla was distilled informally, in the shadow of its famous neighbor — locals kept it alive until the law caught up. This profile covers the Sierra style around the Sierra Occidental.
profiles.description: Sierra raicilla is typically cooked in above-ground adobe ovens rather than pits, so it tends to be less smoky than pit-roasted agave spirits, with a distinctive fermented, gently funky character: orchard fruit, herbs and a soft lactic roundness from wild-yeast fermentation in wooden vats. Distillation happens in small rustic tabernas — the word names the distillery itself, not the still — and each maestro's batches vary widely.
profiles.plant: Agave maximiliana (wild-harvested; Sierra raicilla's signature agave)
profiles.process: Above-ground adobe-oven roast, open wild-yeast fermentation in wooden vats, small-batch distillation
profiles.category: Raicilla — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Jalisco and Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, since 2019)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to raicilla? Expect an agave spirit that is often funkier and fruitier than tequila, and usually lighter on smoke than mezcal — Sierra versions especially. Jalisco's other pride, in a glass.
profiles.smoke: Usually light in the Sierra style: above-ground ovens give a faint roast note rather than pit smoke.
profiles.finish: Medium-long, gently funky, with orchard fruit and a soft sweet-agave fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; its gentle funk also works in a Negroni-style serve (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: Wild maximiliana from Jalisco's mountains, roasted in above-ground adobe ovens rather than pits — less smoke than pit traditions — then open-fermented in wooden vats and small-batch distilled. The rustic herbal edge follows from wild plant, oven roast and batch scale.

profiles.title: Tuxca, Liñeno/Cimarrón style (Jalisco–Colima borderlands)
profiles.context: Tuxca is a borderlands spirit: a traditional agave distillate of the southern-Jalisco/northern-Colima frontier, named for the municipality of Tuxcacuesco below the Volcán de Colima. It has no denomination of origin, and the tradition itself keeps the name regional rather than legal — definitions are loose, and that looseness is part of how the communities around Tuxcacuesco, the Río Almería valley, Zapotitlán de Vadillo and Tolimán keep it: the old way, and quietly.
profiles.description: Tuxca is defined less by a legal category than by its method: wild agaves (often Liñeno/Cimarrón, i.e. Agave angustifolia and relatives) roasted in cylindrical pits, hand-mashed, fermented in volcanic stone craters, and distilled in wooden Filipino stills. The result is lean, spicy and mineral rather than smoky-sweet.
profiles.plant: Wild agaves, often Liñeno/Cimarrón (Agave angustifolia and local relatives); ensambles vary by vinatero
profiles.process: Cylindrical pit roast, hand-mash, volcanic crater fermentation, wooden Filipino still distillation
profiles.category: Tuxca — a regional tradition with no denomination of origin; legal status is not equivalent to tequila or mezcal
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tuxca? Expect an uncertified, deeply traditional borderlands spirit — leaner and more mineral than most mezcal, with spice instead of smoke. No DO certification seal on the bottle; other labeling requirements still apply, and the tradition's authority is cultural rather than certified.
profiles.smoke: Usually light: the pit roast is shorter and the wooden stills read herbal-spicy rather than smoky.
profiles.finish: Dry and spicy, with lime and pepper fading to volcanic mineral.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat alongside water; lean and mineral, it suits slow sipping (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: Wild Liñeño/Cimarrón agaves, a cylindrical pit roast, hand-mashing, fermentation in a volcanic crater filter and a wooden Filipino still — an unusually specific method chain that leaves a distinctive cooked-wild character, varying batch to batch with the agave mix.

profiles.title: Comiteco, aguamiel style (Comitán, Chiapas)
profiles.context: Comiteco belongs to Comitán, Chiapas: a sap-derived agave spirit where, instead of cooking harvested agave hearts, producers collect the fresh sap (aguamiel) of the living maguey comiteco, ferment it, and distill it. Since 6 October 2025 the name “Comiteco de Comitán, Chiapas” is protected as an Indicación Geográfica — a legal protection distinct from a denomination of origin — covering a spirit made from maguey comiteco (identified as Agave americana L. in the declaration; some references also name Agave atrovirens) together with cane sugars in the Meseta Comiteca-Tojolabal. Cane sugar alongside the sap is part of the protected definition, and an honest bottle always tells you what is in it.
profiles.description: Because the agave is never cooked, comiteco lacks the roast and smoke of pit-roasted spirits and instead shows a green, lactic, gently herbal character carried over from the fermented sap — closer in character to a distilled pulque than to mezcal, though it is its own tradition. This profile describes the style generally; compositions vary between producers and are disclosed per bottle.
profiles.plant: Maguey comiteco (Agave americana L. per the 2025 IG declaration; some references name Agave atrovirens), cultivated; sap collected from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel collected from the living plant, fermented, distilled — no cooking of the piña
profiles.category: Comiteco — a regional tradition from Comitán, Chiapas, protected since October 2025 as the Indicación Geográfica “Comiteco de Comitán, Chiapas”; an IG is a different legal figure from tequila's or mezcal's denomination of origin
profiles.beginnerNote: New to comiteco? Forget smoke: this is a sap spirit — think green, lactic and herbal, from uncooked agave. Comitán's own tradition, unlike anything to the north.
profiles.finish: Smooth and herbal, with a light earthy fade and no roast character.

pairing.serving: Neat at room temperature, in a small glass; its green, lactic character also suits a meal shared slowly. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.

profiles.whyItTastes: No roast at all: the living maguey comiteco's sap (aguamiel) is collected, fermented and distilled. Everything in the glass follows from that sap path — which is why comiteco reads nothing like a cooked-heart spirit.

profiles.title: Destilado de pulque, Salmiana style (Tlaxcala)
profiles.context: Tlaxcala holds pulque close: it is the heartland of the maguey pulquero. Destilado de pulque is the region's distilled agave-sap spirit — producers of the pulque tradition ferment the aguamiel of the maguey pulquero (Agave salmiana) into pulque, then distill it — the agave is never cooked. Tlaxcala is not part of the mezcal denomination, and destilado de pulque is not a certified category; it is a regional tradition, sold under destilado labels, kept by families for whom distilling pulque is part of the heritage of their hills. Fermented pulque itself (undistilled) is not part of this spirit catalogue.
profiles.description: Distilling a fermented sap rather than a cooked agave mash gives destilado de pulque its signature: fresh, green, lactic and faintly wild, with the vegetal, slightly tangy character of pulque carried into the glass rather than roast or smoke. Reviews note everything from steamed grass and sour-candy acidity to creamed-corn sweetness — a broad, unusual range.
profiles.plant: Maguey pulquero (Agave salmiana); sap collected daily from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel fermented into pulque (about 48 hours), then distilled; the piña is never cooked
profiles.category: Destilado de pulque — a regional tradition; no denomination of origin, and explicitly not mezcal (fermented pulque is not a distilled spirit)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to destilado de pulque? It is distilled pulque — uncooked agave sap, so expect lactic, green, gently sour character unlike any cooked-agave spirit. A taste of Tlaxcala's oldest trade.
profiles.finish: Light and tangy, with lactic and green notes that fade quickly.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat, chilled slightly; its lactic tang suits an open mind (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: Aguamiel from the living maguey pulquero is fermented into pulque (~48 hours) and then distilled; the piña is never cooked. The profile follows the sap, not the roast.

profiles.title: Costa raicilla, coastal style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Raicilla's denomination of origin (2019) spans 16 Jalisco municipalities and one in Nayarit, and editorially splits into two traditions: Sierra (mountain) and Costa (coastal). Coastal raicilla comes from the Cabo Corrientes and Tomatlán area, made mainly with Agave angustifolia (locally chico aguiar) and Agave rhodacantha. Fishermen and farmers on this coast cook their agave in underground pits, the old way — and the coast takes pride in the lean, saline character of its raicilla beside the mountain style.
profiles.description: Unlike the Sierra style's above-ground adobe ovens, coastal producers traditionally cook their agave in underground pits — so coastal raicilla leans smokier and more savory than its mountain sibling, with the pit roast alongside citrus and herbal notes. This profile describes the editorial style; individual bottles vary widely and tasting notes for the example bottle are not yet documented.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia (chico aguiar) and Agave rhodacantha (wild and cultivated)
profiles.process: Underground pit roast, wild-yeast fermentation, small-batch distillation
profiles.category: Raicilla — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Jalisco and Bahía de Banderas, Nayarit, since 2019); Costa is an editorial tradition split, not a legal class
profiles.beginnerNote: New to coastal raicilla? Think of it as the maritime, more smoky-pit cousin of Sierra raicilla: same DO, different cook. The coast's own take.
profiles.smoke: More present than in Sierra raicilla: the underground pit cook gives a savory smoke woven through citrus and herbs.
profiles.finish: Medium-long, smoky and savory with a citrus fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; the smoke suits slow evening sipping (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: Coastal chico aguiar and rhodacantha agaves, an underground pit roast and wild fermentation in the Cabo Corrientes canyons — a different plant mix and roast from the Sierra tradition, which is why Costa and Sierra raicilla diverge.

profiles.title: Reposado tequila, Tequila Valley style
profiles.context: Reposado ('rested') is a legal tequila class: the spirit rests in oak for a minimum of two months, with no maximum. In practice most producers rest it two months to a year. This profile describes a traditionally made Tequila Valley reposado — the same style as the valley blanco, plus oak. Valley tradition holds that rest should season the agave, never bury it; that restraint is local pride.
profiles.description: Reposado is where tequila first meets wood: the vegetal, peppery blanco character takes on vanilla, caramel and baking-spice notes from the barrel while the cooked agave stays at the center. In traditionally made reposados the oak is a seasoning, not the dish — reviewers of the example bottle consistently note the agave remains forward. There is no universal age-to-flavor ladder: a 2-month reposado can read leaner than a blanco from another producer, and 'more oak' is not 'better'.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked, fermented, double distilled, then rested in oak barrels (legal minimum 2 months; typically 2–12 months)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; reposado is a legal class (oak-rested, 2-month minimum)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to reposado? Think of it as the same spirit as blanco, briefly rested in oak: the agave stays, vanilla and spice join.
profiles.finish: Medium, with gentle wood spice and a caramel-agave fade.

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass, or over one ice cube; its rounder base also carries a Margarita or Paloma well when you want the oak along. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.

profiles.whyItTastes: The same valley base as the blanco, rested in oak for the legal minimum of two months (typically 2–12): the oak softens the vegetal edge and adds gentle spice, without erasing the cooked agave underneath.

profiles.title: Añejo tequila, Tequila Valley style
profiles.context: Añejo ('aged') is a legal tequila class: oak rest of at least one year, in barrels of no more than 600 liters. Extra añejo (at least three years) exists as a further class. This profile describes a traditionally made Valley añejo of roughly 18 months — comfortably past the one-year minimum, which is the only legal mark (the NOM sets a minimum, not a range). Valley practice favors restraint: the agave should still speak through a year of oak, and the best producers make sure it does.
profiles.description: A year or more of oak turns tequila darker, rounder and sweeter-perceived: the barrel contributes vanilla, dried fruit and cocoa-adjacent notes while the fresh vegetal edge of the blanco recedes. A well-made añejo keeps cooked agave in the frame rather than disappearing into wood; the example bottle's reviewers describe exactly that balance. 'Older is better' is marketing, not a rule — wood influence depends on barrel type, size, age and climate, and many drinkers prefer blanco or reposado.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked, fermented, double distilled, then aged in oak at least one year (typically ex-bourbon casks)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; añejo is a legal class (oak-aged, 1-year minimum)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to añejo? Expect the roundest, darkest tequila expression: oak-driven vanilla and dried fruit around the agave — closest to whiskey in feel, still tequila at heart.
profiles.finish: Long and rounded, with oak spice, sweet agave and a gentle dry fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat, ideally in a small glass to concentrate the aroma (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: One year or more in oak (typically ex-bourbon casks): the wood now speaks clearly — vanilla and caramel over the agave — but 'older is better' is marketing, not a rule of flavor.

profiles.title: Cristalino tequila style
profiles.context: Cristalino is not a legal class: it is an aged tequila (usually reposado or añejo) filtered — typically through wood charcoal — to remove the color the barrel gave it. Nearly every major brand now makes one. The category is commercially booming and critically debated: bartenders and writers are divided over whether it is innovation or a marketing-driven dilution of tradition — and that debate is itself part of how Mexico argues, with pride, about its spirits.
profiles.description: A cristalino looks like a blanco in the glass but carries softened barrel character: rounder, creamier and often sweeter-perceived than either a blanco or its unfiltered aged base, with gentler acidity and agave bite. Filtration removes color and, with it, some flavor — what remains is by design smooth and approachable. The category is prone to additive use to restore sweetness and body, which critics flag; the base spirit and the producer matter more than the style name.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated)
profiles.process: Made as oak-rested reposado or añejo, then charcoal-filtered clear; a finishing choice, not a legal class
profiles.category: Cristalino — a finishing/marketing style on top of a legal class, not a legal class itself; disclosure of the aged base varies by brand
profiles.beginnerNote: New to cristalino? It is an aged tequila with the color filtered out — clear like a blanco, rounder like an añejo, and the subject of honest debate.
profiles.finish: Smooth and short-to-medium; engineered for easy sipping.

placeCoords.precision: region (Jalisco, highlands/valley varies by producer); approximate

pairing.serving: Served neat or over ice; often positioned as an entry to aged tequila (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: Made as an oak-rested reposado or añejo and then charcoal-filtered clear: the filtration removes color and, with it, some flavor. What remains is wood-influenced but visually blanco — a finishing choice, not a legal class.

maturation.duration: aged base (varies; typically añejo or extra añejo) then filtered

profiles.title: Comiteco añejo, glass-rested with oak branches (Comitán, Chiapas)
profiles.context: Comiteco is a sap-derived agave spirit from the municipality of Comitán, Chiapas, produced by fermenting and distilling the fresh sap (aguamiel) of the living maguey comiteco without cooking the plant. This profile covers the aged expression of that tradition. The añejo of the example producer rests in glass with branches of white oak rather than in barrels, so its wood character comes from oak contact in glass, not barrel maturation. Añejo here is a producer expression — verify against the applicable IG rules for “Comiteco de Comitán, Chiapas” (protected 6 October 2025) rather than assuming aged classes do not exist.
profiles.description: Glass resting on white-oak branches gives this style a soft wood influence without the vanilla-heavy roundness of barrel-aged spirits: the green, lactic, herbal sap character of comiteco stays in the frame while oak contributes gentle spice and a touch of color. Compared with the unaged comiteco profile, expect a slightly rounder, warmer version of the same tradition rather than a whiskey-adjacent profile.
profiles.plant: Maguey comiteco (Agave americana L. per the 2025 IG declaration; some references name Agave atrovirens), cultivated; sap collected from the living plant
profiles.process: Sap-derived: aguamiel collected from the living plant, fermented, distilled in copper, then rested in glass with branches of white oak (no barrel maturation, no cooking of the piña)
profiles.category: Comiteco añejo — a regional tradition from Comitán, Chiapas, protected since October 2025 as the Indicación Geográfica “Comiteco de Comitán, Chiapas”; añejo here is a producer expression, not a legal class as it is in tequila
profiles.beginnerNote: New to comiteco añejo? Do not expect tequila añejo: the wood comes from oak branches resting in glass, so it is gentler — think warm spice over the same green, lactic sap character.
profiles.finish: Medium-length and herbal, with a soft oak-spice fade and no roast character.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat to let the gentle oak spice carry the herbal sap character (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: Sap-derived like the blanco, then rested in glass with branches of white oak — a gentle wood touch without barrel maturation, and añejo here is a producer expression, not a legal class like tequila's.

profiles.title: Raicilla reposado, barrel-rested style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Raicilla is a denomination-of-origin agave spirit from Jalisco, and aged expressions exist (the example bottle rests in wood); the precise aged-class requirements rest on the 2019 DO declaration and the published standard project rather than tequila-style rules. This profile covers the young-rested end — short rests of a few months that round the spirit without pushing the agave out of the frame. Jalisco's raicilleros are proud that their spirit earned legal recognition without giving up its rustic character; short rests are how they keep it that way.
profiles.description: A short barrel rest (the example bottle lists 3 months) takes the fruity, floral, delicately smoky raicilla character and adds a light wood halo: vanilla, caramel and soft fruit sweetness around — rather than instead of — the agave. Reviewers of the example bottle describe sherry-cask influence with plum, raisin and sweet tobacco, and note the agave can be overpowered by cask character; that risk of wood masking the spirit is part of this style's honest picture.
profiles.plant: Varies by bottling (the example bottle lists Angustifolia and Maximiliana); linked to the Maximiliana plant page as the Sierra tradition's signature agave — check the bottle, batches differ
profiles.process: Fermented and distilled (the example bottle lists steel), then rested in wooden barrels about 3 months
profiles.category: Raicilla reposado — an aged-class claim under the raicilla denomination of origin (2019); the aged-class rules rest on the DO declaration and the published standard project, so verify the effective version rather than assuming tequila-style minimums
profiles.beginnerNote: New to aged raicilla? Expect the fruit and florals of the joven with a light caramel-vanilla halo from a short rest — closer to its unaged self than to tequila reposado.
profiles.smoke: A delicate smokiness can persist from production; the example bottle's reviewer notes campfire smoke on the finish.
profiles.finish: Medium to long, with sweet fruit, cinnamon-adjacent spice and a soft smoke fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; a short-rested raicilla also works where a fruity reposado is called for (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: Fermented and distilled (the example bottle lists steel), then rested in wooden barrels about three months — a short rest of the example bottle (not a legal minimum) that rounds the raicilla without turning it into something else.

profiles.title: Extra añejo tequila, highland style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Extra añejo ('extra aged') is the newest legal tequila class: a minimum of three years in oak barrels of no more than 600 liters, added to the NOM in 2006. It exists because producers wanted recognition for long-rested tequilas; El Tesoro's family released its Paradiso in 1994, before the class legally existed. This profile describes a highland extra añejo of four to five years — well past the three-year minimum, which is the only legal mark (the NOM sets a minimum, not a range). Highland pride runs deep here: growers describe highland agave as bigger and sweeter, and some alteños argue it carries long oak rests better than valley agave — the guide records that as a local view and a tendency, not a rule; valley distilleries also age extra añejo.
profiles.description: Three-plus years of oak pushes tequila toward brandy territory: deep oak, chocolate, coffee and dried fruit around a cooked-agave core. The honest tension of this class is that many producers consider more than about four years excessive — wood can overwhelm the delicate agave — so the best extra añejos are those that keep agave in the frame, as the example bottle's reviewers note. 'Older is better' remains marketing, not a rule.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated; highland mineral soils)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked (or stone-roasted by some traditionalists), fermented, double distilled, then aged at least three years in oak (typically American ex-bourbon barrels)
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; extra añejo is a legal class (oak-aged, 3-year minimum, barrels up to 600 liters)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to extra añejo? This is tequila at its most whiskey-adjacent: expect oak, chocolate and coffee — the good ones still taste of agave underneath.
profiles.finish: Long and oaky, with chocolate, gentle spice and a slow agave fade.

placeCoords.precision: highlands (Los Altos, near Arandas; example producer La Alteña); approximate

pairing.serving: Sipped neat after dinner, in a snifter-style glass (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: Highland agave from red mineral soils tends to read sweeter and more floral than valley agave — a documented tendency, not a guaranteed outcome of place; three-plus years in (typically American ex-bourbon) oak pushes the spirit firmly into wood territory while the highland fruit holds on underneath.

profiles.title: Mezcal reposado, briefly barrel-rested espadín style (Valles Centrales, Oaxaca)
profiles.context: Reposado is a legal mezcal class under NOM-070-SCFI-2016 (which defines six classes: blanco o joven, madurado en vidrio, reposado, añejo, abocado con and destilado con): a rest of two months to a year in wood. Most mezcal sold worldwide is joven (unaged), and many Oaxacan traditionalists argue wood obscures what makes mezcal distinct — that argument is part of the pride: they defend their pit roast because it is their land in the glass. Aged mezcal is nonetheless a growing, legal part of the category. This profile covers the short-rested end: a few months in wood, typically starting from pit-roasted espadín.
profiles.description: A short barrel rest softens the pit-roast smoke of espadín mezcal and layers light vanilla and caramel over it, without erasing the spirit's vegetal, roasted character. Reviews of the example bottle describe exactly that balance — smoke carried from nose to finish, ending in a smoky butterscotch — while others caution the wood can dominate. Expect mezcal first, wood second; if the wood leads, it is closer to tequila reposado territory.
profiles.plant: Agave angustifolia (espadín, cultivated); some producers blend wild agaves
profiles.process: Pit-roasted, stone-milled, wild-fermented, distilled, then rested in oak 2-12 months (the example bottle lists 4-6 months in American oak)
profiles.category: Mezcal — spirit with its own denomination of origin; reposado is a legal class (wood-rested, 2–12 months; the wood need not be oak, and the two-month start coincides with tequila's although the other requirements differ)
profiles.beginnerNote: New to mezcal reposado? Expect the smoke of a joven softened with vanilla and caramel — a gentler entry into smoked agave spirits.
profiles.smoke: The pit-roast smoke of espadín mezcal persists through the rest; reviewers describe it from nose to finish.
profiles.finish: Medium, smoky-sweet, with a butterscotch-adjacent fade.

placeCoords.precision: region (Tlacolula valley, Valles Centrales, Oaxaca); approximate

pairing.serving: Sipped neat; also works in margaritas where a smoky reposado is welcome (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: The same pit-roasted espadín base as the joven, rested in oak 2–12 months (the example bottle lists 4–6 in American oak): the roast stays, softened by wood. Tequila and mezcal reposado both start at two months, but their other requirements differ — do not transfer rules between spirits.

profiles.title: Tobalá mezcal, wild Agave potatorum style (Sierra, Oaxaca)
profiles.context: Tobalá (Agave potatorum) is a small, high-altitude, mostly wild agave often called the 'king of agaves' in México; its tiny size and long maturity (a variable, source-dependent range often cited around 12–15 years) give very low yields, which has pushed prices up and wild populations down. The mezcal DO permits any agave species, so tobalá is mezcal; some tobalá is now cultivated, which changes both the sustainability story and, reviewers note, sometimes the flavor. This is a plant-driven style, not a place-driven one: tobalá grows across Oaxaca's Sierra Norte and beyond. In the Sierra Norte, finding a tobalá ready to harvest is a source of personal pride — a mezcalero will walk you to the plant, not to a map.
profiles.description: Tobalá mezcal is typically lighter and more floral than espadín, with sweet citrus, tropical fruit and a silky texture over a gentler roast. Batch variation is genuinely large — a cited blind tasting of eight tobalás found no single common thread — so treat this as a family of expressions, not one flavor. The example bottle, from wild-harvested tobalá around Santiago Matatlán, is herbal and delicate, with dry soil, thyme, coriander and a touch of rosemary.
profiles.plant: Agave potatorum (tobalá; mostly wild-harvested, some cultivated — check the bottle)
profiles.process: Pit-roasted, stone-milled, wild-fermented, distilled; NOM-070's artisanal category permits copper alembics or clay pots, so clay is not exclusive to ancestral production
profiles.category: Mezcal — tobalá is within the mezcal denomination of origin; it is a wild agave category under sustainability pressure, not a legal class of its own
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tobalá? Expect mezcal's gentler, more floral cousin: sweet citrus and tropical fruit over a soft roast — pricier because the agave is small, slow and scarce.
profiles.smoke: A gentle roast character rather than heavy smoke; ancestral clay-pot batches can show more.
profiles.finish: Medium and silky, with fruit sweetness and a soft mineral fade.

placeCoords.precision: region (Sierra Norte de Oaxaca; the wild style ranges across the Sierra, while the example bottle is produced in Santiago Matatlán); approximate

pairing.serving: Neat in a small copita — a small stemmed glass — so the florals gather; if you mix it, expect a quieter, gentler version rather than the whole character. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.

profiles.whyItTastes: Small wild tobalá matures over a variable, source-dependent range (often cited around 12–15 years) at altitude, giving very low yields; reviewers describe concentrated character in some batches, pit roast and often clay-pot distillation keep the cook gentle. Batch variation is genuine and large — a cited blind tasting found no single common thread.

profiles.title: Sotol, Chihuahua desert style
profiles.context: Ask a sotolero what sotol is and you will hear it plainly: not agave, and proud of it. Sotol is distilled from plants of the Dasylirion genus (desert spoon), native to the Chihuahuan desert — relatives of agave in the Asparagaceae family that share the roasted-piña logic. Sotol has had a Denominación de Origen since 2002, covering only Chihuahua, Coahuila and Durango; its 20th-century history includes restrictive regulation and clandestine production (the specific legal timeline varies by era and place; this guide does not assert a single nationwide pre-1994 ban). This guide includes it as an agave-adjacent tradition, honestly labeled: sotol is not an agave spirit, and saying so is part of its story. This profile describes the Chihuahua desert style.
profiles.description: Sotol's signature is a bright, grassy, herbal, sometimes menthol- or eucalyptus-adjacent freshness — more vegetal than most agave spirits, with a smoky, earthy base from pit roasting. Terroir is unusually audible: the cited DO sources describe forested-region sotols tasting of menthol, mushrooms and pine, while arid-desert ones lean to leather, cacao and pepper. A single plant may yield roughly one bottle after a variable, source-dependent number of years (often cited around 8–12), so batches are small and vary genuinely.
profiles.plant: Dasylirion (desert spoon; commonly wheeleri, cedrosanum or leiophyllum), wild-harvested; not an agave, though a close relative
profiles.process: Piña pit-roasted in conical ovens (or steam-cooked by larger producers), wild-fermented, distilled in copper or clay; whether roots are left intact depends on harvest practice, and regrowth is not guaranteed
profiles.category: Sotol — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin (Chihuahua, Coahuila, Durango, since 2002); explicitly not an agave spirit, included here as an agave-adjacent northern tradition
profiles.beginnerNote: New to sotol? Expect bright wet-grass and herbal freshness over gentle smoke — closer to a green, wild cousin of mezcal than to tequila.
profiles.smoke: A gentle, usually lighter smoke than mezcal from the pit roast; batch and producer dependent.
profiles.finish: Medium, herbal and slightly tingly, with a mineral fade.

pairing.serving: Sipped neat in a small glass; also good with mineral sparkling water (editorial suggestion).

profiles.whyItTastes: Dasylirion (not an agave) wild-harvested, pit-roasted in conical ovens and wild-fermented: the earthy, smoky-herbal character follows from the plant and the desert cook. Wild stands face documented harvest pressure; regrowth claims need species and method evidence this guide has not verified.

profiles.title: Highland blanco tequila, Los Altos style (Jalisco)
profiles.context: Blanco is the unaged legal class of tequila — and the highlands (Los Altos) around Atotonilco el Alto and Arandas read it very differently from the Tequila Valley. Red iron-rich mineral soils, higher elevation and cooler nights tend to grow bigger, sweeter agave, so a highland blanco often leans bright, fruity and floral where the valley leans earthy and savory. This is a cultural and agronomic distinction, not a legal class — both are simply tequila blanco, and Los Altos takes visible pride in its red-earth fruitiness.
profiles.description: The highland take on unaged tequila: sweeter cooked agave with citrus (orange peel, grapefruit), tropical and stone fruit, delicate florals and a gentle spice, in a softer, rounder body than the valley style.
profiles.plant: Agave tequilana Weber azul (blue weber agave, cultivated; highland red mineral soils)
profiles.process: Steam-cooked (or stone-roasted by some traditionalists), fermented, double distilled; typically unaged, though blanco rules permit brief oak contact below the two-month reposado minimum
profiles.category: Tequila — spirit with its own Denomination of Origin; blanco is a legal class of tequila typically sold unaged, though the rules permit brief oak maturation below the reposado minimum
profiles.beginnerNote: New to tequila? A highland blanco is often described as a friendly starting point: soft, sweet and fruity, and often less savory than a valley blanco — though valley and highland overlap, and individual bottles vary. Try it beside the valley blanco to taste what place can do to the same plant.
profiles.finish: Soft and fruity, with a slow sweet-agave fade and a light peppery lift at the end.

placeCoords.precision: town (Atotonilco el Alto area, Los Altos); approximate

pairing.serving: Neat in a small glass, or in a Margarita/Paloma where its fruit plays well with citrus. Editorial suggestion, not a rule.

profiles.whyItTastes: Los Altos agave grows at higher elevation in red iron-rich soils with cooler nights, and growers say those conditions produce bigger, sweeter piñas — so the unaged spirit leans fruity, floral and citrus-bright rather than earthy. Note the honest caveat: one blind tasting panel found the regional pattern weaker than folklore suggests, so treat this as a tendency, never a guarantee.
